summary.text: Writing $p=2d+1$, Euler’s criterion and a binomial/Vandermonde factorization reduce the even-$d$ case modulo $p$ to nonzero Vandermonde and binomial factors; Wilson’s theorem gives $(d!)^2=(-1)^{d+1}$, which makes the remaining two-term factor nonzero.  For odd $d$, reindexing by the nonzero quadratic residues expresses the matrix as an odd number of columns from a skew-symmetric group-circulant matrix and the rest from a commuting symmetric one (the odd count follows from the product of the relevant quadratic characters), forcing the determinant to vanish; finally $d$ is odd exactly when $p\equiv3\pmod4$.

full_proof.text:
Let \(p_n\) denote the \(n\)-th prime, with \(p_1=2,p_2=3,\ldots\). For \(n\geq 2\), put
\[
p=p_n,\qquad d=\frac{p-1}{2},\qquad C=d!.
\]
Thus \(p\) is an odd prime and \(p=2d+1\). Let \(\chi\) be the quadratic character of \(\mathbb F_p\), extended by \(\chi(0)=0\). The integer matrix defining the sequence is
\[
M=(M_{ij})_{1\leq i,j\leq d},\qquad
M_{ij}=\left(\frac{i^2-Cj}{p}\right)=\chi(i^2-Cj).
\]
We prove the following stronger prime-by-prime assertion:
\[
\det M=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad d\text{ is odd}.
\]
Since \(p=2d+1\), the condition that \(d\) is odd is equivalent to \(p\equiv3\pmod4\). This will prove the conjecture.

We use throughout the elementary half-factorial consequence of Wilson's theorem
\[
(C\bmod p)^2=(-1)^{d+1}\quad\text{in }\mathbb F_p. \tag{1}
\]
For completeness, Wilson's theorem gives
\[
\prod_{a=1}^{p-1}a=-1\quad\text{in }\mathbb F_p.
\]
Split the product into \(1,\ldots,d\) and \(d+1,\ldots,2d\). Under the bijection \(a\mapsto p-a\), the second half has product
\[
\prod_{a=d+1}^{2d}a=\prod_{b=1}^{d}(-b)=(-1)^dC.
\]
Consequently \(C((-1)^dC)=-1\), which rearranges to (1).

We first prove nonvanishing when \(d\) is even.

Consider a general field \(F\), elements \(x_1,\ldots,x_d,y_1,\ldots,y_d\in F\), and suppose
\[
x_i^d=1\qquad(1\leq i\leq d). \tag{2}
\]
We need a factorization of the determinant
\[
D=\det\bigl((x_i-y_j)^d\bigr)_{1\leq i,j\leq d}. \tag{3}
\]
Let \(V_x=(x_i^r)\), where columns are indexed by \(r=0,1,\ldots,d-1\). By the binomial theorem and (2),
\[
(x_i-y_j)^d
 =1+(-1)^dy_j^d+
 \sum_{r=1}^{d-1}x_i^r(-1)^{d-r}\binom dr y_j^{d-r}.
\]
Therefore the matrix in (3) factors as \(V_xE\), where the rows of \(E\) are indexed by \(r=0,\ldots,d-1\), and
\[
E_{0j}=1+(-1)^dy_j^d,
\]
while, for \(1\leq r\leq d-1\),
\[
E_{rj}=(-1)^{d-r}\binom dr y_j^{d-r}. \tag{4}
\]
Extract from row \(r\) of \(E\), for each \(r>0\), the scalar
\[
q_r=(-1)^{d-r}\binom dr,
\]
and put \(q_0=1\). What remains is a matrix whose first row is
\(1+(-1)^dy_j^d\), and whose other rows are \(y_j^{d-r}\).
By linearity of the determinant in the first row, its determinant is the sum of two determinants. The part with first row \(1\), after reversing the order of the remaining \(d-1\) rows, is a Vandermonde determinant in the \(y_j\)'s, up to a sign \(\varepsilon\in\{1,-1\}\). The part with first row \(y_j^d\) has a factor \(y_j\) in each column; after extracting all these factors and reversing all \(d\) rows, it is again a Vandermonde determinant, up to a sign \(\delta\in\{1,-1\}\). Hence
\[
D=\det(V_x)\left(\prod_{r=0}^{d-1}q_r\right)
 \left(\varepsilon+(-1)^d\delta\prod_{j=1}^dy_j\right)
 \det(V_y), \tag{5}
\]
where \(V_y=(y_j^r)_{j,r}\) is the usual Vandermonde matrix. The precise values of \(\varepsilon\) and \(\delta\) will not matter; only \(\varepsilon^2=\delta^2=1\) is needed.

Apply (5) in \(F=\mathbb F_p\) with
\[
x_i=i^2,\qquad y_j=Cj\qquad(1\leq i,j\leq d). \tag{6}
\]
First, Fermat's theorem gives
\[
x_i^d=(i^2)^d=i^{p-1}=1,
\]
because \(1\leq i<p\), so (2) holds.

The \(x_i\)'s are pairwise distinct. Indeed, if \(i^2=j^2\pmod p\), then \(p\mid(i-j)(i+j)\). Since \(1\leq i,j\leq d\), we have \(0<i+j\leq2d=p-1\), so \(p\nmid i+j\); hence \(p\mid i-j\), and therefore \(i=j\). Thus \(\det(V_x)\ne0\).

The \(y_j=Cj\) are also pairwise distinct. The number \(C=d!\) is nonzero modulo \(p\), since all of its factors are smaller than \(p\). Therefore multiplication by \(C\) is injective, and the residues \(C,2C,\ldots,dC\) are distinct. Thus \(\det(V_y)\ne0\).

Each row scalar \(q_r\) is nonzero modulo \(p\). This is immediate for \(q_0=1\). For \(1\leq r<d<p\),
\[
\binom dr=\frac{d!}{r!(d-r)!}
\]
is nonzero in \(\mathbb F_p\), because all factorials occurring here are products of nonzero residues and hence are invertible. Therefore \(\prod q_r\ne0\).

It remains to prove that the final parenthesis in (5) is nonzero when \(d\) is even. Set
\[
Y=\prod_{j=1}^dy_j.
\]
Using (6),
\[
Y=\prod_{j=1}^d(Cj)=C^d d!=C^{d+1}. \tag{7}
\]
If \(d\) is even, (1) says \(C^2=-1\). Consequently
\[
Y^2=C^{2(d+1)}=(C^2)^{d+1}=(-1)^{d+1}=-1. \tag{8}
\]
Also \((-1)^d=1\). If the final factor in (5) vanished, we would have
\(\varepsilon+\delta Y=0\), hence \(Y=-\varepsilon\delta\), and squaring would give \(Y^2=1\). This contradicts (8), because \(p\) is odd and hence \(1\ne-1\) in \(\mathbb F_p\). Thus every factor in (5) is nonzero, and
\[
\det\bigl((i^2-Cj)^d\bigr)_{1\leq i,j\leq d}\ne0
\quad\text{in }\mathbb F_p. \tag{9}
\]

Euler's criterion, including the case where the argument is zero, states that
\[
\chi(a)=a^{(p-1)/2}=a^d\quad\text{in }\mathbb F_p.
\]
Therefore the reduction modulo \(p\) of the integer Legendre-symbol matrix \(M\) is exactly the power matrix in (9). If the integer \(\det M\) were zero, its reduction modulo \(p\) would be zero, contradicting (9). Hence
\[
d\text{ even}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\det M\ne0. \tag{10}
\]

We now prove vanishing when \(d\) is odd. This part rests on a structural determinant lemma.

Let \(G\) be a finite abelian group, let \(f,g:G\to\mathbb Q\), and define their group-circulant matrices by
\[
K_{ab}=f(ab^{-1}),\qquad S_{ab}=g(ab^{-1})\qquad(a,b\in G).
\]
Suppose
\[
f(u^{-1})=-f(u),\qquad g(u^{-1})=g(u) \tag{11}
\]
for all \(u\in G\). Then \(K^T=-K\) and \(S^T=S\). Moreover, all group-circulant matrices on a finite abelian group commute. Indeed, their products are convolution matrices, and convolution is commutative on an abelian group. Thus \(KS=SK\).

We claim that if \(T\subseteq G\) has odd cardinality, then the matrix formed by taking column \(b\) from \(K\) for \(b\in T\), and from \(S\) for \(b\notin T\), has determinant zero. First suppose \(S\) is invertible. Since \(K\) and \(S\) commute, they also commute with \(S^{-1}\). Put \(L=S^{-1}K\). Then
\[
L^T=K^T(S^{-1})^T=(-K)S^{-1}=-S^{-1}K=-L,
\]
so \(L\) is skew-symmetric. The mixed-column matrix factors as \(SN\), where column \(b\) of \(N\) is column \(b\) of \(L\) if \(b\in T\), and is the \(b\)-th column of the identity if \(b\notin T\). Reorder rows and columns so that the elements of \(T\) come first. Then \(N\) has block form
\[
N=\begin{pmatrix}L_{T,T}&0\\ *&I\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The principal block \(L_{T,T}\) is skew-symmetric of odd order. Its determinant equals the determinant of its transpose, but
\[
\det(L_{T,T}^T)=\det(-L_{T,T})=(-1)^{|T|}\det(L_{T,T})=-\det(L_{T,T}),
\]
so, over \(\mathbb Q\), its determinant is zero. Hence \(\det N=0\), and the mixed determinant is zero.

No invertibility assumption on \(S\) is actually needed. Replace \(S\) by \(S+tI\). This remains symmetric and still commutes with \(K\). For all but finitely many rational \(t\), \(S+tI\) is invertible, since \(\det(S+tI)\) is a nonzero monic polynomial in \(t\). The corresponding mixed-column determinant is itself a polynomial in \(t\), and by the preceding argument it vanishes for every rational \(t\) outside a finite set. A polynomial over \(\mathbb Q\) with infinitely many roots is zero, so evaluating at \(t=0\) proves the claim for the original \(S\).

We apply this lemma to the group \(G=H\) of nonzero squares in \(\mathbb F_p\). This is a subgroup of \(\mathbb F_p^\times\), and it has order \(d=(p-1)/2\). The map
\[
\{1,\ldots,d\}\longrightarrow H,\qquad i\longmapsto i^2 \tag{12}
\]
is a bijection. Injectivity was proved above. Surjectivity follows because every nonzero square has two square roots \(r\) and \(-r\), exactly one of whose standard representatives lies in \(\{1,\ldots,d\}\).

For the columns, put
\[
y_j=Cj\in\mathbb F_p^\times.
\]
Because now \(p\equiv3\pmod4\), \(-1\) is a nonsquare, or equivalently
\[
\chi(-1)=-1. \tag{13}
\]
Define
\[
c_j=\begin{cases}
y_j,&y_j\text{ is a square},\\-y_j,&y_j\text{ is a nonsquare}.
\end{cases} \tag{14}
\]
Every \(c_j\) belongs to \(H\): this is clear in the first case, and in the second case (13) gives
\(\chi(-y_j)=\chi(-1)\chi(y_j)=(-1)(-1)=1\).

The map \(j\mapsto c_j\) from \(\{1,\ldots,d\}\) to \(H\) is injective. The residues \(y_j=Cj\) are pairwise distinct. Also, one can never have \(y_i=-y_j\), because cancellation of the nonzero \(C\) would give \(i+j\equiv0\pmod p\), while
\(2\leq i+j\leq2d=p-1\). Thus equality between two values selected according to (14), in any of the four possible square/nonsquare cases, forces the original indices to be equal. Since both sets have \(d\) elements, this map is a bijection.

Let
\[
T=\{c_j:y_j\text{ is a square}\}\subseteq H. \tag{15}
\]
We next show that \(|T|\) is odd. Since \(d\) is odd, (1) gives \(C^2=1\). From (7),
\[
\prod_{j=1}^dy_j=C^{d+1}=(C^2)^{(d+1)/2}=1. \tag{16}
\]
Applying the multiplicative character \(\chi\) to (16) gives
\[
\prod_{j=1}^d\chi(y_j)=1.
\]
Every \(y_j\) is nonzero, so every factor is \(1\) or \(-1\). Therefore the number of nonsquare \(y_j\)'s is even. Since the total number \(d\) is odd, the number of square \(y_j\)'s is odd. The column map is injective, so (15) indeed has odd cardinality.

Define two rational-valued functions on \(H\) by
\[
f(u)=\chi(u-1),\qquad g(u)=\chi(u+1),
\]
regarding the integer values \(-1,0,1\) of \(\chi\) as rational numbers. For \(u\in H\), both \(u\) and \(u^{-1}\) are squares, so \(\chi(u^{-1})=1\). The identities
\[
u^{-1}-1=-(u-1)u^{-1},\qquad
u^{-1}+1=(u+1)u^{-1}
\]
and (13) therefore give
\[
f(u^{-1})=-f(u),\qquad g(u^{-1})=g(u). \tag{17}
\]
Thus the group-circulant matrix built from \(f\) is skew-symmetric, the one built from \(g\) is symmetric, and they commute.

Index the rows by \(r=i^2\in H\) using (12), and index the columns by \(c=c_j\in H\) using (14). If \(y_j\) is a square, then \(c_j=y_j\), and the entry in the \(f\)-circulant column is
\[
f(rc_j^{-1})
 =\chi(rc_j^{-1}-1)
 =\chi((r-y_j)c_j^{-1})
 =\chi(r-y_j), \tag{18}
\]
because \(c_j^{-1}\) is a square. If \(y_j\) is a nonsquare, then \(c_j=-y_j\), and the entry in the \(g\)-circulant column is
\[
g(rc_j^{-1})
 =\chi(rc_j^{-1}+1)
 =\chi((r+c_j)c_j^{-1})
 =\chi((r-y_j)c_j^{-1})
 =\chi(r-y_j), \tag{19}
\]
again because \(c_j\in H\). Thus, after the two bijective reindexings, the matrix \(M\) is precisely the mixed-column matrix that uses the skew-circulant column for the columns in \(T\), and the symmetric-circulant column for those outside \(T\).

The set \(T\) has odd cardinality, so the mixed group-circulant determinant lemma applies and gives
\[
d\text{ odd}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\det M=0. \tag{20}
\]
Although the circulant argument was phrased over \(\mathbb Q\), this is exactly the same determinant: all entries are the rational images of the integers \(-1,0,1\). A determinant of an integer matrix is zero if and only if its image in \(\mathbb Q\) is zero.

Combining (10) and (20), for every odd prime \(p=2d+1\),
\[
\det_{1\leq i,j\leq d}\left(\frac{i^2-d!j}{p}\right)=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad d\text{ is odd}.
\]
Finally,
\[
d\text{ odd}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
2d+1\equiv3\pmod4
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
p\equiv3\pmod4.
\]
For \(n\geq2\), the prime \(p_n\) is odd and the sequence term \(a(n)\) is exactly the integer determinant above with \(p=p_n\) and \(d=(p_n-1)/2\). Hence
\[
\boxed{\ a(n)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p_n\equiv3\pmod4\ }
\]
for every \(n\geq2\), as claimed.
